blocks.content: The jurisdiction conferred on the High Courts under Article 226 is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

rows: Enforcement of Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights
Mandatory (Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right)
Narrower per case, but applies across the whole territory of India
Wider in scope, but territorially restricted to the State or UT jurisdiction

items: Article 226 covers both Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights, whereas Article 32 is restricted only to Fundamental Rights.
Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, making it mandatory for SC to entertain it, while Article 226 is a discretionary power of the High Court.
In the L. Chandra Kumar case (1997), the Supreme Court held that the writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is an integral part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose' (ordinary legal rights).
The five types of writs available under Article 226 are Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-Warranto.
The writ jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 is wider than the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 32.
An aggrieved person can approach a High Court directly under Article 226 without first approaching lower subordinate courts.
The remedy provided under Article 226 is discretionary; the High Court may refuse to grant relief if alternative effective remedies exist.
